title: Light & Weather
summary: Snow, fog, storm clouds and low autumn sun: how painters from Goya and Shōhaku to Monet and Inness learned to paint the air itself.
description:
Weather is the one subject every viewer already knows by heart. We have all watched a storm roll in over a beach, squinted through river mist or trudged across fresh snow. **Light & Weather** brings together fifteen works from the collection in which the real subject is not a place but a condition: the temperature of the light, the weight of the sky, the hour of the day.

## Snow and silence

Winter has a way of simplifying the world, and artists have long used it to strip a picture down to essentials. Around 1786 Francisco Goya painted travellers struggling along an icy road in a snowstorm, one of a series of studies for royal tapestries of the four seasons; diagonal strokes of grey and white seem to drive the snow across the canvas.

{{artwork:93450}}

In Japan, Soga Shōhaku took an even bolder route around 1761–62, painting a snow-covered Mount Fuji in negative: the white of the mountain is simply bare paper, outlined in ink wash. A century later, Camille Pissarro recorded the brutal French winter of 1879 at Pontoise in thick, frothy paint, and John Henry Twachtman, who believed that "never is nature more lovely than when it is snowing," found quiet contemplation in the frozen landscape around his Connecticut home.

{{artwork:271418|inset}}

## Chasing the changing sky

The nineteenth century turned weather into a laboratory. John Constable sketched the Suffolk countryside with a palette knife, flecking the surface with white to catch sparkling wetness. Eugène Boudin, Monet's teacher, set up his easel on the beach and painted an approaching storm over holidaymakers in 1864, and his habit of working outdoors would shape a generation.

No one pursued the idea further than Claude Monet. In 1890–91 he painted the wheat stacks outside his Giverny farmhouse again and again, working at several easels at once as the light shifted from autumn afternoon to winter sunset. The collection's group of these canvases lets you compare the same motif under completely different skies.

{{artwork:14624}}

Monet later painted his Mornings on the Seine from a boat anchored at dawn, numbering the canvases so he could move from one to the next as the mist lifted, and in London he rose early to paint Waterloo Bridge dissolving in fog, a city he said would not be beautiful without it.

## Mood and atmosphere

For some painters, weather was less about observation than feeling. James McNeill Whistler's spare seascape at Trouville and his Nocturne of Southampton Water reduce sea and sky to broad bands of tone, closer to music than to description. George Inness, late in his career, sought what he called "poetic truth": in Early Morning, Tarpon Springs, blurred outlines and a solitary figure evoke the hush of a Florida dawn.

{{artwork:64729|inset}}

Seen together, these works remind us that light is never neutral. It carries season, temperature and emotion, and the artists here spent their lives learning to paint something no one can hold: the air between us and the world.

title: Small Worlds
summary: Coins, amulets, votive brooches, a rosary bead and rooms built at one-twelfth scale: an exhibition of tiny objects that carry enormous meaning.
description:
Some of the most powerful objects in the collection could fit in the palm of your hand. **Small Worlds** gathers seventeen of them, from silver coins struck in Greek city-states to amulets worn by Egyptians and miniature rooms built in twentieth-century Chicago. Their size invites a closer look, and online you can zoom in further than you ever could through a display case.

## Power in your pocket

Coins were the mass media of the ancient world. A city chose its emblem carefully: the island of Aegina stamped its silver with a sea turtle while it ruled the waves, and after its defeat by Athens in 458 BCE switched to a land tortoise. Neapolis in northern Greece honoured Medusa, mother of the winged horse Pegasus, because the city was famous for horse breeding.

{{artwork:142732}}

Rome transformed the coin into a portrait gallery. In 44 BCE Julius Caesar became the first living person to appear on Roman coinage, and from then on rulers' profiles became standard. The exhibition includes a denarius portraying Caesar, a gold aureus of Hadrian, a tetradrachm pairing Cleopatra VII with Mark Antony, with the queen on the front as the more important of the two, and a rare solidus of the Byzantine empress Irene, one of only three women to hold sole power in that empire.

{{artwork:221685|inset}}

## Protection and prayer

In Egypt, small figurines called amulets were thought to promote health and luck, and they were worn by the living and the dead. A glass amulet from Akhenaten's reign shows Taweret, the hippopotamus goddess of childbirth; a faience group presents Isis and Nephthys flanking the young Horus, promising renewal after death. A gold ring pairs Isis nursing Horus with a visual pun on its owner's name, Horemakhbit, meaning "Horus in the Marsh."

{{artwork:64167}}

The Greeks offered small bronzes to their gods: brooches, beads and figurines hung from sacred trees or placed in sanctuaries, then ceremonially buried when a shrine filled up. Two thousand years later, a Flemish carver fitted an entire Crucifixion inside a wooden rosary bead of about 1500–25, meant to inspire wonder during private prayer.

## Worlds in miniature

Other small objects are pure delight. A seventeenth-century jewel turns a lumpy baroque pearl into a cat holding a mouse. Nineteenth-century Baccarat paperweights capture botanical specimens in glass, answering a European craze for collecting and classifying nature.

{{artwork:45360|inset}}

Finally, Narcissa Niblack Thorne's miniature rooms reconstruct historical interiors in astonishing detail. Borrowing tricks from stage design, she turned chairs outward in her Pennsylvania kitchen so that nothing blocks the view, and filled her Louis XVI salon with the roses Marie Antoinette loved. Step close, and a whole world opens up.

title: The Art of Adornment
summary: Earrings, eye paint, gold pectorals, silver belts and painted finery: 3,500 years of how people have decorated themselves, and why it mattered.
description:
What we wear says who we are, or who we want to be. **The Art of Adornment** explores personal decoration across the collection, from Egyptian glass earrings and kohl jars to Andean gold, Navajo silver and the painted silks and chains of European portraiture. Some of these objects were made for beauty, some for status and some for protection, and many for all three at once.

## Made to be worn

In New Kingdom Egypt, men, women and children of every social class wore earrings. The collection holds a matched pair of blue glass hoops, made around 1400–1295 BCE by wrapping hot glass around a rod and fusing it with a twisted cane of white and black.

{{artwork:840}}

Egyptians also lined their eyes with kohl, both for beauty and, it seems, to cut the glare of the North African sun, storing it in small containers like a travertine jar that was buried with its owner for use in the afterlife. Around the Mediterranean, a gold Greek earring ends in a tiny dolphin's head, and a Roman necklace of the second or third century hangs an emerald from a finely woven chain, fastened with a garnet rosette that only an upswept hairstyle would reveal.

## Mirrors and meaning

Adornment starts with looking at yourself. An Egyptian bronze hand mirror joins its disk to a papyrus-shaped handle, evoking the sun rising from the marsh; the Egyptian words for mirror and life sounded alike. An Etruscan mirror of the third century BCE has a handle in the form of a winged Lasa, an attendant of the goddess of love.

{{artwork:213732|inset}}

In the ancient Americas, ornament signalled cosmic as well as social rank. A Chavín gold pectoral of about 500 BCE combines human and animal features, expressing the priestly rulers' bond with natural forces. Coclé goldsmiths cast paired caiman-like creatures as pendants, evoking the land floating in the primordial sea. Much later, in the 1880s, Navajo (Diné) silversmiths, who had learned the craft from Hispanic artisans in New Mexico, developed the distinctive concho belt.

{{artwork:184361}}

## Dressed for the portrait

Painters knew that clothes and jewellery could tell a sitter's story. Frans Hals caught the sheen of black satin in his 1627 Portrait of a Lady. Rembrandt dressed a favourite model in a gold chain and steel gorget to suggest an honoured military past. Ingres's Comte de Pastoret wears his finest garments and the medal of the Legion of Honour, while John Singer Sargent set off Mrs. George Swinton's regal bearing with bursts of brushwork describing a shimmering gown.

{{artwork:95998|inset}}

Even armour became fashion: a sixteenth-century suit from Augsburg imitates, in etched steel, the embroidered front of a gentleman's doublet. From glass hoops to gilded steel, adornment turns the body into a place where craft, identity and belief meet.

title: Monsters & Marvels
summary: Griffins, dragons, gorgons, ghosts and demon-quellers: a closed exhibition on the creatures humans invented to name their fears and guard their dead.
description:
Every culture has its monsters. **Monsters & Marvels** gathered sixteen works from the collection in which artists gave shape to the things that frighten us, and to the fierce protectors summoned to keep those things at bay. The exhibition has now closed, but every work remains available to explore in the collection.

## Guardians with claws

Many of the oldest creatures here were on our side. Around 625–575 BCE, Greek bronzeworkers cast a pair of griffins, part eagle, part lion, to decorate a great cauldron offered at a sanctuary. Griffins were revered for their ferocity and protective power, and these still keep some of their inlaid eyes.

{{artwork:129906}}

In Tang dynasty China, a haughty armoured guardian stood near a tomb chamber to repel evil, and a sancai-glazed amphora of the early 700s has handles in the form of dragons biting its rim. In the American Southwest, Ancestral Pueblo potters painted horned serpents, associated with the life-giving power of water, stretching across a jar.

## Dragons, devils and the hero's fight

Sometimes the monster must be defeated. Bernat Martorell's Saint George of 1434–35 spears a scaly dragon modelled in raised stucco, and a fifteenth-century Spanish sculpture shows the archangel Michael battling the devil. Albrecht Dürer's engraving Knight, Death, and the Devil of 1513 is subtler: the knight rides on, unafraid, as Death holds up an hourglass and a devil trails behind.

{{artwork:11100|inset}}

In Japan, Soga Shōhaku painted a dragon rising in storm clouds over Mount Fuji, stirring up wind and rain around the boats below. Kawanabe Kyōsai's 1887 triptych shows Shōki the Demon Queller riding a tiger that clutches a goblin in its jaws, an image traditionally hung for the Boys' Day festival in May.

{{artwork:271417}}

## Ghosts and the gaze

The exhibition closed with the most unsettling monsters of all, the ones that look like us. Hokusai's series One Hundred Ghost Tales, of 1831–32, includes Oiwa, disfigured by poison and emerging from a paper lantern to take revenge; the skeletal Kohada Koheiji peering through a mosquito net at the couple who murdered him; and the ghost of a woman drowned in a well for breaking plates. Hokusai's bright blue, cheerful to modern eyes, was associated by his audience with death and the occult.

{{artwork:47403|inset}}

In Europe, Antonio Canova's plaster head of Medusa, with blank eyes and snakes caressing her cheeks, reverses the gorgon's deadly gaze, and Henry Fuseli painted heads inspired by the damned souls of Dante's Inferno. Monsters, the exhibition suggested, are never only about fear. They are how people have named danger, honoured protection and imagined what lies beyond the edge of the known.
